claims.text: Inherent chemical complexity in multi-component concentrated alloys increases spatial fluctuations in local stacking- or shear-fault energy.
Local fault-energy fluctuations promote deformation twinning over conventional slip.
Local fault-energy fluctuations produce hard atomic motifs that impede or pin dislocations.
Fluctuations in shear-fault energy are a primary origin of strength in complex concentrated alloys.
Twinning and dislocation pinning caused by fault-energy fluctuations delay failure.
Metastable Fe80−xMnxCo10Cr10, CrMnFeCoNi, and CrCoNi alloys exhibit chemistry-dependent deformation twinning.
The proposed initial alloy is an FCC random solid solution with natural chemical inhomogeneities.
Annealing temperature and cooling rate can selectively increase or decrease chemical short-range order without changing overall composition.
Thermally changing short-range order will tune the magnitude of local stacking-fault-energy fluctuations.
Decreasing temperature can drive metastable multi-component alloys between different deformation modes.
At ambient-to-cryogenic temperatures and moderate strain rates, both slip and twinning are active and sensitive to the local energy landscape.
Spatial variations in local fault energy cause wavy or otherwise unusual dislocation behavior.
Hard atomic motifs preferentially promote deformation twinning.
Twinning dissipates strain energy and thereby delays catastrophic failure.
The proposed mechanism simultaneously enhances yield strength and ductility.
Increasing chemical short-range order will increase local fault-energy fluctuations.
Samples with enhanced short-range order will have greater yield strength than homogenized samples with minimal short-range order.
Samples with enhanced short-range order will have a higher deformation-twin density than the baseline.
Minimizing short-range order produces a more uniform fault-energy landscape and conventional dislocation-controlled deformation.
The mechanism should apply primarily to metastable FCC concentrated alloys with low-to-moderate stacking-fault energies and need not govern stable or BCC alloys.
